## feature

### QUALITY_ENCODING_AMBIGUOUS warning replaces the hard rejection

```
level: high
```

#### reason

The end-to-end test proves the new behavior on the reviewer's own example: a uniform-Q60 (`]`) file previously aborted the run (exit 2); it now completes, produces the finding, and yields a REVIEW decision that withholds automatic approval.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. The classic Phred+64 signature — whole-file every quality byte ≥ 64 with some ≥ 90 — is valid under BOTH encodings: Sanger FASTQ encodes Phred 0–93 as ASCII 33–126 ([Cock et al., 2010](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/38/6/1767/3112533)), so Q60 is valid Phred+33 input and the same bytes are routine Q26+ under Phred+64.
2. The scan no longer raises on the signature: `FastqFileStats.encoding_ambiguous` records it per strand under the declared Phred+33 reading.
3. `policy._metadata_findings` emits one WARNING per affected dataset naming both readings, the computed-under-+33 fact, and the resolution (verify the encoding at its source; a Phred+64 file must be re-exported, never modified); metadata status becomes REVIEW, so the decision is REVIEW and `QUALITY_ENCODING_AMBIGUOUS` reaches the reason codes.
4. Bytes outside [33, 126] still abort — the provable violation, unchanged. No override flag, no declaration machinery, no Phred+64 support.

#### before

A valid-if-unusual Phred+33 file (whole-file uniform-high qualities) aborted the run with no processing path, and the rejection asserted "probably Phred+64" as certainty — the pretense the specification forbids.

#### after

Ambiguity is recorded, reported, and decision-visible: the group can never be COMPATIBLE while the doubt stands, and the operator receives a full report instead of an error.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

`tests/test_e2e.py::test_ambiguous_encoding_warns_and_withholds_approval` (finding, metadata REVIEW, decision REVIEW, reason code); `tests/test_fastq.py::test_ambiguous_signature_flags_not_rejects` (flag set for `bytes([64,70,80,104])`, unset for uniform `K`); `test_quality_outside_ascii33_126_rejected` unchanged and passing.

:::

## limitation

### v1 reads every input as Phred+33; Phred+64 stays unsupported

```
level: medium
```

#### reason

Restated because the new warning makes the boundary visible: ambiguous files are processed under +33, not converted.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. A genuine Phred+64 file now flows through with a warning and +31-shifted absolute quality statistics; relative comparisons still function, and cross-encoding groups show enormous quality distances that flag themselves.
2. Supporting +64 (detection or conversion) remains a future feature per the specification ("For v1, explicitly support Phred+33").

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

:::

## assumption

### The user confirmed overriding two earlier confirmed decisions

```
level: high
```

#### reason

The heuristic was kept by confirmed disposition in rounds 2 and 3; round 4's reframing changed the analysis, and the user confirmed the reversal.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Three considerations moved the position: the specification's rejection criterion is input "known to violate" the encoding (the signature is suspicion, not knowledge); a hard rejection asserts a guess symmetric to the silent-acceptance guess the design rejects; and conditional on the signature firing in 2026, the file is more likely uniform-high Phred+33 (simulators, fixtures) than GAIIx-era Phred+64.
2. The corruption risk that justified rejection is contained: it requires extinct-format input, mixed groups self-flag through quality distances, and the warning surfaces the doubt on every affected decision.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

Disposition message 2026-10-22 (agreement-first analysis); `/tmp/spec_seqc.md` spec wording; user confirmation "Go ahead."

:::

## observation

### The reviewer softened P1 to P2, matching our own frequency analysis

```
level: medium
```

#### reason

Both sides converged on the practical-impact assessment from opposite directions.

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Round 2 argued the rejection window is effectively synthetic-only; the round-4 review concedes ordinary production files rarely hit it ("calling it universally release-blocking was too strong").
2. The disagreement that remained — what to do when the window does fire — is what the confirmed design resolves.

## process

### reversed a twice-confirmed position on a better argument

```
status: right
```

#### description

```
type: [text]
```

1. Rounds 2 and 3 defended the heuristic with the corruption scenario and the spec's fail-fast class; each defense was evidence-based at the time.
2. Round 4's reframing (declared-reading semantics; the rejection itself asserts a guess; conditional-on-firing frequency) was stronger, and the honest response was to update the recommendation — presented to the user with the reasoning explicit, then implemented only after confirmation.
3. The lesson recorded: re-examine the framing of a rejected argument, not only its facts, when it returns.

#### evidence

```
level: high
type: [text]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

Disposition messages of rounds 2, 3, and 4; user confirmations in the session log.

:::
